notes.text: for the sake of My servant This title is used in the Torah only of the patriarchs, Moses, and Caleb. Very few individuals in the rest of the Bible, of whom David is the outstanding one, are called "My servant." The righteous are collectively termed "the servants of the Lord," and in Isaiah 40-66, there appears the enigmatic figure of the "servant of the Lord," whose suffering is seen to be part of the process of Israel's national redemption. The significance of the title becomes clear from the description of Caleb: "He was imbued with a different spirit and remained loyal to Me" (Num. 14:24). In the face of widespread disaffection and demoralization, Caleb displayed superior moral courage, unswerving loyalty, and heroic leadership. (Nahum Sarna, The JPS Torah Commentary: Genesis, Philadelphia, 1989, 187).

the God of your father This epithet, used here for the first time, is distinctively character- istic of the subsequent patriarchal narratives…In the present context, the designation affirms God's role as the guarantor of the promises: He is the same One who spoke with Abraham. At the same time, it emphasizes the continuity of the succession from father to son, and it connotes a personal and intimate relationship between God and the individual. (Nahum Sarna, The JPS Torah Commentary: Genesis, Philadelphia, 1989, 187).
